fuentes/ultimatum-saraiva-1864/titulo.texto: Saraiva's Ultimatum to the Government of Uruguay

fuentes/ultimatum-saraiva-1864/resumen.texto: Note that the special envoy of the Empire of Brazil, José Antônio Saraiva, delivered on August 4, 1864 to the White government of Atanasio Aguirre. It demanded the punishment of those responsible and compensation for the damages that, according to the Empire, Brazilian subjects had suffered on the border, and warned that otherwise Brazilian forces would act on their own.

fuentes/ultimatum-saraiva-1864/por_que_i.texto: Its rejection opened the Brazilian military intervention in Uruguay in support of Venancio Flores, which Paraguay regarded as a threat and which set off the War of the Triple Alliance.

fuentes/nota-paraguaya-de-1864/titulo.texto: Note from the Paraguayan Government to the Brazilian Representative (August 30, 1864)

fuentes/nota-paraguaya-de-1864/autor.texto: José Berges, foreign minister of Paraguay

fuentes/nota-paraguaya-de-1864/resumen.texto: Note from Paraguayan foreign minister José Berges to the Empire's representative in Asunción, sent after Saraiva's ultimatum became known. It declared that Paraguay would regard any occupation of the Eastern territory by Brazilian forces as an attack on the balance among the States of the Plate, which mattered to it as a guarantee of its own security.

fuentes/nota-paraguaya-de-1864/por_que_i.texto: It is the direct diplomatic antecedent of the capture of the Marquis of Olinda and of the invasion of Mato Grosso; López's defenders cite it as proof that Paraguay warned before acting.

fuentes/tratado-de-la-triple-alianza/aut.texto: Governments of Argentina, the Empire of Brazil and Uruguay

fuentes/tratado-de-la-triple-alianza/res.texto: Secret treaty signed in Buenos Aires on May 1, 1865 by Rufino de Elizalde for Argentina, Francisco Octaviano de Almeida Rosa for Brazil and Carlos de Castro for Uruguay, after the Paraguayan invasion of Corrientes. The allies committed themselves not to lay down arms until they overthrew the government of Francisco Solano López and not to sign a separate peace, and they declared that the war was against that government and not against the Paraguayan people, whose independence they guaranteed. They set in advance the postwar boundaries of Paraguay (for Argentina, Misiones and the Chaco up to Bahía Negra; for Brazil, up to the Apa River), the demolition of the Humaitá fortifications and payment of the war costs by Paraguay.

fuentes/tratado-de-la-triple-alianza/por.texto: It defined the allies' war aims and was the most debated document of the conflict: its publication in London in 1866 fueled opposition to the war and protests from other American governments, and its boundary clauses were renegotiated after 1870.

fuentes/tratado-de-la-triple-alianza/lee.texto: Text of the treaty on Wikisource

fuentes/manifiesto-de-felipe-varela/titu.texto: Manifesto to the American Peoples on the Political Events of the Argentine Republic in the Years 1866 and 1867

fuentes/manifiesto-de-felipe-varela/resu.texto: Manifesto dated in Potosí on January 1, 1868, under the motto “¡Viva la Unión Americana!”, in which Varela, already defeated and exiled in Bolivia, justified his rebellion. He holds that the war with Paraguay was prepared by Mitre in agreement with the Empire of Brazil, which had invaded Uruguay to support Flores, and he denounces the governments imposed on the provinces and the forced conscription of contingents; he thus takes up the proclamation with which he had risen in December 1866.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-felipe-varela/por_.texto: It is the main text of the federal opposition from the interior to the Paraguayan War and a central piece of the revisionist reading of those years.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-felipe-varela/leer.texto: Text of the 1868 manifesto on Wikisource

fuentes/el-crimen-de-la-guerra/resumen.texto: Essay that Alberdi wrote in Europe in 1870 and that was published after his death, in his Posthumous Writings (1895). It argues that war between nations is a crime, that it is justified only as self-defense, that its responsible parties are rulers and not peoples, and it proposes a society of nations with an international tribunal; it includes criticisms of the Paraguayan War and of the alliance with Brazil.

fuentes/el-crimen-de-la-guerra/por_que_i.texto: It is the main Argentine expression of nineteenth-century juridical pacifism and part of Alberdi's critique of the war conducted by Mitre.

fuentes/grandes-y-pequenos-hombres-del-p.texto: Great and Small Men of the Plata

Writings by Alberdi from the 1860s and 1870s, published posthumously in Paris in 1912. They discuss Argentine history as Mitre wrote it and criticize Mitre, Sarmiento and the policy of Buenos Aires, which Alberdi accuses of having kept the customs house and the port at the expense of the provinces.
It was widely used by later revisionism as a liberal counter-history opposed to Mitre's.

fuentes/vida-del-chacho/titulo.texto: Biographical Sketches of General Ángel V. Peñaloza (Life of the Chacho)

fuentes/vida-del-chacho/resumen.texto: Articles that José Hernández published in the newspaper El Argentino of Paraná at the end of 1863, weeks after Peñaloza's death, and later gathered into a pamphlet. They present the Chacho as a popular and generous caudillo, denounce his killing after he had surrendered as a crime of the liberal party, and warn Urquiza that he was in the same danger.

fuentes/vida-del-chacho/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main contemporary federal source on the death of the Chacho and anticipates the defense of the gaucho in Martín Fierro.

fuentes/el-chacho-sarmiento/titulo.texto: The Chacho, Last Caudillo of the Montonera of the Llanos

fuentes/el-chacho-sarmiento/resumen.texto: Sarmiento's account of Peñaloza's uprisings of 1862 and 1863, in which he himself acted as governor of San Juan and director of the war. Published in 1868 together with a new edition of Facundo, it presents the montonera as a remnant of rural barbarism and justifies the repression and the death of the caudillo.

fuentes/el-chacho-sarmiento/por_que_impo.texto: It is the version of the main civil official responsible for the campaign against the Chacho and the counterpoint to Hernández's Life of the Chacho.

fuentes/el-chacho-sarmiento/leer.0.titul.texto: Civilization and Barbarism: Lives of Quiroga, Aldao and the Chacho (1889), on Internet Archive

fuentes/codigo-civil-1869/titulo.texto: Civil Code of the Argentine Republic (Law 340)

fuentes/codigo-civil-1869/resumen.texto: Code drafted by Dalmacio Vélez Sarsfield between 1864 and 1869 on commission from Mitre's government, drawing on Roman law, the French code, Teixeira de Freitas's project for Brazil and the Chilean code, and approved by Congress without debate, sight unseen, by Law 340 of September 25, 1869. It took effect on January 1, 1871 and regulated persons, family, contracts, property and inheritance; marriage remained in the hands of the Church until 1888.

fuentes/codigo-civil-1869/por_que_import.texto: It was the basis of Argentine private law until 2015, when the Civil and Commercial Code replaced it.

fuentes/ley-1029-de-federalizacion/titul.texto: Law 1029 on the Federalization of Buenos Aires

fuentes/ley-1029-de-federalizacion/resum.texto: Law of September 1880, passed after the defeat of the province of Buenos Aires in the June revolution, which declared the city of Buenos Aires the capital of the Republic. Its transfer to the nation was made subject to acceptance by the provincial legislature, which voted it in November of that year.

fuentes/ley-1029-de-federalizacion/por_q.texto: It closed the question of the capital, open since the 1820s, and left the customs house and the port of Buenos Aires to the nation.

fuentes/ley-1029-de-federalizacion/leer..texto: Text of the law on Wikisource

fuentes/ley-universitaria-1885/resumen.texto: Law of 1885, proposed by Nicolás Avellaneda as senator and rector of the University of Buenos Aires, which set the bases for the statutes of the national universities of Córdoba and Buenos Aires. It gave them self-government, with a superior council and faculties led by academics, and left to the Executive the appointment of professors from shortlists.

fuentes/ley-universitaria-1885/por_que_i.texto: It governed university life until 1947, and its system of closed academies was one of the targets of the 1918 University Reform.

fuentes/codigo-penal-1886/autor.texto: Congress of the Nation, based on the project of Carlos Tejedor

fuentes/codigo-penal-1886/resumen.texto: First national penal code, passed in 1886 on the basis of the project that Carlos Tejedor had drafted in the 1860s on commission from the national government, and in force from 1887. It kept the death penalty and was amended several times until its replacement by the 1921 code.

fuentes/codigo-penal-1886/por_que_import.texto: It unified the criminal legislation of the country, which until then was governed by Spanish laws and by Tejedor's project as adopted in several provinces.

fuentes/ley-de-bancos-garantidos-1887/re.texto: Law of 1887, from the presidency of Juárez Celman, which allowed banks, including provincial ones, to issue banknotes backed by national debt securities bought with gold. Several provinces took loans abroad to buy those securities, and the issue of paper money grew very fast.

fuentes/ley-de-bancos-garantidos-1887/po.texto: The expansion of credit and issue that it made possible lies at the center of the speculation that ended in the 1890 crisis.

fuentes/ley-de-matrimonio-civil-1888/res.texto: Law passed in November 1888, during the presidency of Juárez Celman, which replaced the chapter of the Civil Code that recognized only religious marriage. It established that the only marriage with legal effects was the one celebrated before the civil registry officer, regardless of the religion of the parties, and it admitted legal separation but not divorce that dissolves the marriage bond.

fuentes/ley-de-matrimonio-civil-1888/por.texto: Together with Law 1420 and the civil registry, it completed the secularization of institutions that the Catholic Church fought in the 1880s; it remained in force, with reforms, until the divorce law of 1987.

fuentes/exposicion-de-del-valle-1890/res.texto: Letter-account of 1890 addressed to Francisco A. Barroetaveña, one of the founders of the Unión Cívica, in which Aristóbulo del Valle recounts from within the preparation of the Parque revolution: the plan to arrest the president, the vice president, the minister of war and Roca, the uprising of July 26 and the armistice negotiations. He also explains why the civil leaders accepted surrender.

fuentes/exposicion-de-del-valle-1890/por.texto: It is the most detailed testimony of one of the leaders of the 1890 revolution, which gave rise to the Radical Civic Union.

fuentes/ley-de-conversion-1899/resumen.texto: Law of 1899, from Roca's second presidency and of his finance minister José María Rosa, which set the value of the paper peso at 44 gold centavos and charged the Conversion Office with exchanging gold for banknotes at that price. It halted the appreciation of the paper peso, which harmed exporters.

fuentes/ley-de-conversion-1899/por_que_i.texto: It established the gold standard that governed until World War I.

fuentes/ley-de-servicio-militar-1901/res.texto: Organic military law of 1901, prepared by War Minister Pablo Riccheri during the tension with Chile. It established compulsory conscription of Argentine men aged 20, with a lottery to determine who served and in which branch, and reorganized the army.

fuentes/ley-de-servicio-militar-1901/por.texto: Compulsory military service remained in force until 1994, and military enrollment was used from 1911 as the basis of the electoral roll.

fuentes/proyecto-de-ley-nacional-del-tra.texto: Draft labor code that Interior Minister Joaquín V. González sent to Congress in 1904, with Roca's signature, prepared with collaborators of different tendencies, among them socialists, and drawing on data from the Bialet Massé report. It regulated the labor contract, the working day, Sunday rest, the work of women and minors, accidents, unions and the conciliation of disputes, and at the same time included controls on foreigners and workers' associations.
It never came up for debate: it was rejected by both employers' and workers' organizations, but many of its parts became laws in the following decades.

fuentes/ley-de-descanso-dominical/resume.texto: Law of 1905 that prohibited, in the Federal Capital, work for wages on Sundays, with exceptions for services that could not be interrupted. It gathered bills from the socialist deputy Alfredo Palacios and also had the support of Catholic deputies.

fuentes/ley-de-descanso-dominical/por_qu.texto: It was one of the country's first labor laws.

fuentes/ley-de-trabajo-de-mujeres-y-meno.texto: Law 5291 on Work by Women and Minors

Law of 1907, based on a bill by the socialist deputy Alfredo Palacios and on the 1904 draft national labor law, which regulated the work of women and minors in the Capital. It set a minimum working age, limited the working day of minors, restricted night work and work in unhealthy tasks, and gave female workers a rest after childbirth.
It was the first Argentine law protecting female and child labor.

fuentes/ley-de-defensa-social/resumen.texto: Law passed at the end of June 1910, days after the bomb that exploded at the Colón Theatre, under the state of siege of the Centennial. It prohibited the entry into the country of anarchists and of those convicted of common crimes, prohibited associations and meetings that spread anarchism, and punished with prison, and with death in certain attacks, those who used explosives or praised such crimes.

fuentes/ley-de-defensa-social/por_que_im.texto: Together with the Residence Law, it was the main legal instrument against the anarchist movement.

fuentes/ley-de-enrolamiento/resumen.texto: Law of 1911, sent by Roque Sáenz Peña and his minister Indalecio Gómez, which ordered a new military enrollment of all men and made it the basis of the electoral roll, which until then had been compiled by local authorities. With Law 8130, which placed the roll under federal justice, it prepared the secret and compulsory voting law of 1912.

fuentes/ley-de-enrolamiento/por_que_impo.texto: It removed control of the electoral roll from provincial governments and local caudillos, one of the bases of electoral fraud.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-saenz-pena-1912/ti.texto: Manifesto of President Roque Sáenz Peña to the People of the Republic

fuentes/manifiesto-de-saenz-pena-1912/re.texto: Message that the president addressed to the country at the end of February 1912, after promulgating Law 8871 and before the first elections with secret and compulsory voting. It promises the government's non-interference in the elections, calls on citizens to vote and ends with the exhortation that became the most quoted phrase of the reform: “let the people vote.”

fuentes/manifiesto-de-saenz-pena-1912/po.texto: It sums up the political purpose of the Sáenz Peña law: to replace fraud and abstention with parties and competitive elections.

fuentes/tratado-de-limites-1881/titulo.texto: Boundary Treaty between Argentina and Chile (1881)

fuentes/tratado-de-limites-1881/resumen.texto: Treaty signed in Buenos Aires on July 23, 1881 by Foreign Minister Bernardo de Irigoyen and the Chilean consul Francisco de Borja Echeverría, with mediation by the representatives of the United States in both countries, while Chile was at war with Peru and Bolivia. It fixed the boundary along the Andes, by the highest peaks dividing the waters, up to the 52nd parallel; it left eastern Patagonia to Argentina and the Strait of Magellan, neutralized, to Chile, and it divided Tierra del Fuego by a meridian.

fuentes/tratado-de-limites-1881/por_que_.texto: It closed Chile's claim over Patagonia, but the difference between the line of the highest peaks and the watershed divide gave rise to the disputes that followed.

fuentes/tratado-de-limites-1881/leer.0.t.texto: Text of the treaty on Wikisource

fuentes/pactos-de-mayo/resumen.texto: Three agreements signed in Santiago on May 28, 1902 that ended the crisis of the arms race: a preliminary act on the policy of both countries in the Pacific and the Atlantic, a general arbitration treaty and a convention limiting naval armaments. Under the latter, the two governments gave up the warships they were building in Europe, which were later sold.

fuentes/pactos-de-mayo/por_que_importa.texto: They settled by arbitration and naval limitation the conflict that had come close to war in 1898–1902; the Christ the Redeemer of the Andes (1904) commemorates that peace.

fuentes/pactos-de-mayo/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text of the pacts on Wikisource

fuentes/nota-drago/titulo.texto: Note from Foreign Minister Drago to the Government of the United States (Drago Doctrine)

fuentes/nota-drago/resumen.texto: Note dated December 29, 1902 that Foreign Minister Luis María Drago sent to the Argentine minister in Washington, Martín García Mérou, to present it to the government of the United States during the blockade of Venezuela. It holds that the public debt of a state cannot justify armed intervention or the occupation of its territory by a foreign power, and asks that the United States recognize it as a complement to the Monroe Doctrine.

fuentes/nota-drago/por_que_importa.texto: The 1907 Hague Conference approved a softened version (the Drago-Porter Convention), which prohibited the use of force to collect debts unless the debtor refused arbitration.

fuentes/derecho-internacional-teorico-y-.texto: Theoretical and Practical International Law of Europe and America

Treatise on international law published in Paris in 1868, in two volumes, and expanded in later French editions. It upholds the sovereign equality of states and rejects the use of force or diplomatic protection by the powers to back the claims of their citizens against an American state: foreigners must submit to local courts like nationals.
It is the origin of the Calvo Doctrine and of the “Calvo clause,” which many Latin American states included in their contracts and constitutions.
Volume 1 of the 1868 edition on Internet Archive

fuentes/fausto-del-campo/titulo.texto: Faust. Impressions of the Gaucho Anastasio el Pollo at a Performance of This Opera

fuentes/fausto-del-campo/resumen.texto: Gauchesco poem of 1866 in which the gaucho Anastasio el Pollo tells his friend Laguna, in the language of the countryside, about the performance of Gounod's opera Faust that he saw at the Colón Theatre, convinced that what was happening onstage was real.

fuentes/fausto-del-campo/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most popular works of gauchesco poetry and an example of its humorous use by city writers.

fuentes/santos-vega-ascasubi/titulo.texto: Santos Vega or The Twins of the Flower

fuentes/santos-vega-ascasubi/resumen.texto: Long gauchesco poem published in Paris in 1872, in which the legendary payador Santos Vega tells the story of two twin brothers, one honest and the other criminal, in the Buenos Aires countryside at the end of the colonial period. It includes extensive descriptions of rural life, of the estancias and of the malones.

fuentes/santos-vega-ascasubi/por_que_imp.texto: It fixed the legend of Santos Vega in writing, a legend later taken up by Rafael Obligado and other poets.

fuentes/la-vuelta-de-martin-fierro/resum.texto: Second part of José Hernández's poem, published in 1879. Martín Fierro returns from the toldos, where he lived among the Indigenous peoples, is reunited with his children and with Cruz's son, and in the payada with the Moreno and in his final counsel to his sons he preaches prudence, work and respect for the law.

fuentes/la-vuelta-de-martin-fierro/por_q.texto: Much criticism reads in it, unlike La ida (1872), which denounced abuses against the gaucho, a reconciliation with the order of the time of Avellaneda and Roca. Since Lugones's 1913 lectures (El payador) and Ricardo Rojas's work, the two parts have been considered the Argentine national poem.

fuentes/juan-moreira/resumen.texto: Novel published as a serial in the newspaper La Patria Argentina between 1879 and 1880, based on the life of a real gaucho, Juan Moreira, killed by a police patrol in Lobos in 1874. It presents Moreira as an honest man pushed into crime by the injustices of the justice of the peace and of the caudillos of the countryside, who used him as an electoral thug.

fuentes/juan-moreira/por_que_importa.texto: It was an enormous popular success, passed into the circus and the theater, and set the model of the gaucho hunted by the law.

fuentes/dos-partidos-en-lucha/titulo.texto: Two Parties in Struggle. Scientific Fantasy

fuentes/dos-partidos-en-lucha/resumen.texto: Tale of 1875 that imagines a confrontation in Buenos Aires between the supporters and the opponents of Darwin's theories, with characters who caricature scientists and figures of the time. It satirizes porteño intellectual life and takes the side of evolutionism.

fuentes/dos-partidos-en-lucha/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the first science fiction texts in the country and a record of the arrival of Darwinism in Argentina.

fuentes/la-antiguedad-del-hombre-en-el-p.texto: The Antiquity of Man in the Plata

Two-volume work published in 1880 and 1881, while Ameghino was in France, in which he brings together his finds of human remains, objects and fossils in the province of Buenos Aires. It holds that human beings coexisted in the pampas with the extinct large mammals and that their presence there was much older than was accepted.
The coexistence of humans with the megafauna was later confirmed, but not the enormous antiquities Ameghino proposed.
Volume 1 of the official edition of Ameghino's works (1918), on Internet Archive

fuentes/omnipotencia-del-estado/titulo.texto: The Omnipotence of the State Is the Negation of Individual Freedom

fuentes/omnipotencia-del-estado/resumen.texto: Speech that Alberdi read on May 24, 1880 at the graduation ceremony of the Faculty of Law of Buenos Aires. It holds that the fatherland and the state inherited from the Greco-Roman tradition absorb the individual, and that modern freedom, of Anglo-Saxon origin, consists in limiting the power of the state over persons, property and labor.

fuentes/omnipotencia-del-estado/por_que_.texto: It is one of the classic texts of Argentine liberalism, still invoked today by liberals and libertarians.

fuentes/conflicto-y-armonias-de-las-raza.texto: Conflict and Harmonies of the Races in America

Sarmiento's last major book, the first volume of which appeared in 1883, in which he tries to explain, with the racial science of his time, why Spanish America had not reached the development of the United States. He attributes the backwardness to the Spanish colonial heritage and to mixture with Indigenous and African peoples, and proposes as remedy education and European immigration.
It shows Sarmiento's turn toward positivism and racialism: positivists invoked it, and those who see in it a justification for the exclusion of Indigenous people and mestizos criticize it.

fuentes/juvenilia/resumen.texto: Book of memories in which Cané recounts his years as a boarding student at the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires in the 1860s: the teachers, among them Amadeo Jacques, the pranks and rebellions of the students and life in the boarding house.

fuentes/juvenilia/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most widely read books of the Generation of '80 and the classic image of the Colegio Nacional as a seedbed of the elite.

fuentes/en-viaje/resumen.texto: Chronicles of Cané's trip as a diplomat to Venezuela and Colombia in 1881 and 1882, with stops in Europe and the Caribbean. It combines descriptions of landscapes, cities and customs with judgments on Spanish American politics from the liberal, Europhile viewpoint of his generation.

fuentes/en-viaje/por_que_importa.texto: It is a good example of the travel literature of the Generation of '80 and of its way of seeing the other countries of America.

fuentes/la-gran-aldea/resumen.texto: Novel first published as a serial in 1884, in which a narrator recalls the Buenos Aires of the 1860s and compares it with the city of 1880. It satirizes the old porteño society, party politicians and the nouveaux riches, and describes with nostalgia and mockery the passage from the “big village” to the cosmopolitan city.

fuentes/la-gran-aldea/por_que_importa.texto: Its title became the usual way of naming Buenos Aires before the great immigration.

fuentes/sin-rumbo/resumen.texto: Naturalist novel of 1885 about Andrés, a rich, skeptical and bored estanciero who divides his life between the estancia and the city. The seduction of a puestero's daughter, the death of his own daughter and his final suicide show the moral emptiness that the author attributed to the elite of his time.

fuentes/sin-rumbo/por_que_importa.texto: It is considered Cambaceres's best novel and one of the first modern Argentine novels.

fuentes/en-la-sangre/resumen.texto: Naturalist novel of 1887 about Genaro, the son of a poor Neapolitan immigrant, who rises socially through deceit and by marrying a rich young woman, and ends by ruining her family. The novel attributes his conduct to the heritage of his origin and expresses the prejudices of the Creole elite against immigrants.

fuentes/en-la-sangre/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main example of Argentine naturalist fiction and of the elite's reaction to mass immigration.

fuentes/causeries-del-jueves/resumen.texto: Written talks that Mansilla published weekly in the porteño press and collected in five volumes between 1889 and 1890. In a conversational tone they mix memories of his childhood in the time of Rosas, who was his uncle, anecdotes of travel and of political life, and judgments on the society of his time.

fuentes/causeries-del-jueves/por_que_imp.texto: They are among the best examples of the conversational and autobiographical prose of the Generation of '80.

fuentes/la-bolsa/titulo.texto: The Stock Exchange. A Social Study

fuentes/la-bolsa/resumen.texto: Novel published as a serial in La Nación in 1891 about Dr. Glow, a prestigious lawyer who is ruined by speculation on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange during the boom of the 1880s and ends in madness. It explains the 1890 crisis as the work of Jewish and foreign financiers, with explicit anti-Semitism taken from the Frenchman Édouard Drumont, and it is one of the first expressions of that prejudice in Argentine literature.

fuentes/la-bolsa/por_que_importa.texto: It is the novel of the 1890 crisis and a document of the anti-Semitism and xenophobia of part of the porteño elite.

fuentes/mis-montanas/resumen.texto: Book of memories and sketches of 1893 in which González recalls his childhood in the Famatina valley, in La Rioja: the landscape of the sierra, the customs, the legends and the civil wars that the old people of the place used to tell about.

fuentes/mis-montanas/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the founding works of the regional literature of the Northwest and of the idea of an interior that kept the national tradition.

fuentes/la-tradicion-nacional/resumen.texto: Essay of 1888 in which González seeks the roots of Argentine nationality in Indigenous traditions, legends, popular poetry and the history of the colony and of independence. A later edition included a letter from Bartolomé Mitre about the book.

fuentes/la-tradicion-nacional/por_que_im.texto: It was one of the first attempts to found a national identity on tradition, before the cultural nationalism of the Centennial.

fuentes/la-locura-en-la-historia/titulo.texto: Madness in History. A Contribution to the Psychopathological Study of Religious Fanaticism and Its Persecutions

fuentes/la-locura-en-la-historia/resumen.texto: Study of 1895 on religious fanaticism and the Inquisition in Europe, which Ramos Mejía explains as manifestations of mental illness in individuals and peoples. He applies to history the concepts of the positivist psychiatry of his time.

fuentes/la-locura-en-la-historia/por_que.texto: It shows how Argentine medical positivism read history as a pathology, the same method it applied to Rosas and to Argentine crowds.

fuentes/la-locura-en-la-historia/leer.0..texto: 1895 edition digitized by the U.S. National Library of Medicine, on Internet Archive

fuentes/la-bolsa-de-huesos/resumen.texto: Short detective novel of 1896 in which the narrator, a doctor, investigates, starting from a bag of human bones, a series of deaths of medical students, and discovers that they were poisoned by a woman who posed as a student.

fuentes/la-bolsa-de-huesos/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the first Argentine detective novels.

fuentes/del-plata-al-niagara/resumen.texto: Account of the trip Groussac made in 1893 through Chile, Peru, Central America, Mexico and the United States, where he visited the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. It combines chronicle with judgments on North American civilization, which he admires for its energy and criticizes for its materialism.

fuentes/del-plata-al-niagara/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the most widely read travel books of its time and a precursor of the Latin American critique of the United States that Rodó took up in Ariel (1900).

fuentes/las-multitudes-argentinas/resume.texto: Essay of 1899 in which Ramos Mejía applies to Argentine history the crowd psychology of Gustave Le Bon: he interprets the May Revolution, the montoneras and popular support for Rosas as works of crowds guided by instinct. At the end he deals with the immigrant crowds of his time, which he considers malleable through state education.

fuentes/las-multitudes-argentinas/por_qu.texto: It is one of the central works of Argentine positivism and of the elite's view of the masses and immigration.

fuentes/la-ciudad-indiana/titulo.texto: The Indies City. Buenos Aires from 1600 to the Mid-Eighteenth Century

fuentes/la-ciudad-indiana/resumen.texto: Study of 1900 on the colonial society of Buenos Aires: the distribution of land, trade and smuggling, the cabildo, the family, the Church and mentalities. It uses the minutes of the cabildo and other documents to explain Argentine political customs by their colonial origin.

fuentes/la-ciudad-indiana/por_que_import.texto: It is a founding work of Argentine social and economic history, which departed from the political and military history that dominated.

fuentes/nuestra-america-bunge/titulo.texto: Our America. An Essay in Social Psychology

fuentes/nuestra-america-bunge/resumen.texto: Essay published in Barcelona in 1903, with a prologue by Rafael Altamira, which explains the political problems of Spanish America, such as caciquismo, by the character of its peoples, born of the mixture of Spaniards, Indigenous people and Africans. It attributes to those groups fixed psychological traits, such as laziness, sadness and arrogance, and sees the way out in European immigration and education.

fuentes/nuestra-america-bunge/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the most characteristic texts of Latin American positivist racial determinism, much criticized later for that reason.

fuentes/simulacion-de-la-locura/resumen.texto: Study of 1903, developed from his medical thesis, on the simulation of mental illness by defendants in criminal cases and, more generally, on simulation as a form of struggle for life. It rests on the cases Ingenieros attended in the observation service for the insane of the Buenos Aires police.

fuentes/simulacion-de-la-locura/por_que_.texto: It is a central work of Argentine positivist criminology.

fuentes/la-guerra-gaucha/resumen.texto: Book of stories of 1905 about the gaucho guerrillas of Salta and Jujuy who, under the command of Martín Miguel de Güemes, fought the royalist armies in the War of Independence. It is written in a highly elaborate modernista prose with an affected vocabulary.

fuentes/la-guerra-gaucha/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the first works to make the gaucho a national hero, on the path Lugones followed in El payador (1916).

fuentes/la-restauracion-nacionalista/tit.texto: The Nationalist Restoration. Report on Education

fuentes/la-restauracion-nacionalista/res.texto: Report that Rojas presented to the Ministry of Justice and Public Instruction after studying the teaching of history in Europe, published in 1909. It proposes a historical and patriotic education, with the study of national history, geography and language, to give a sense of Argentine identity to the children of immigrants in the face of cosmopolitanism.

fuentes/la-restauracion-nacionalista/por.texto: It is one of the texts that founded the cultural nationalism of the Centennial; Rojas conceived it as a liberal and democratic nationalism, distinct from the authoritarian one that emerged later.

fuentes/teoria-y-practica-de-la-historia.texto: Book of 1909, developed from lectures, in which Justo sets out his interpretation of history from biology and economics, with a personal reading of historical materialism. He defends a reformist socialism that advances through trade-union organization, cooperation and parliamentary action, and not through revolution.
It is the main theoretical work of the founder of the Argentine Socialist Party.

fuentes/el-diario-de-gabriel-quiroga/tit.texto: The Diary of Gabriel Quiroga. Opinions on Argentine Life

fuentes/el-diario-de-gabriel-quiroga/res.texto: Book of 1910 written as the diary of a young Argentine who reflects on the country of the Centennial. It criticizes the materialism and cosmopolitanism of Buenos Aires and of immigration, and proposes recovering the national spirit in the interior provinces, the Hispanic tradition and Catholicism.

fuentes/el-diario-de-gabriel-quiroga/por.texto: Together with Rojas's The Nationalist Restoration, it is one of the first texts of Argentine cultural nationalism.

fuentes/estudio-sobre-las-casas-de-inqui.texto: Study of the Tenement Houses of Buenos Aires

Hygienist study of 1885 on the conventillos of the city of Buenos Aires: overcrowding, lack of light, ventilation and water, and the mortality of their inhabitants, most of them immigrants. Rawson presents them as breeding grounds of epidemics that threatened the whole city, and calls on the state to regulate and promote workers' housing.
It is one of the founding texts of hygienism and of the question of popular housing in Argentina.

fuentes/la-nacion/resumen.texto: Newspaper founded by Bartolomé Mitre on January 4, 1870, successor to La Nación Argentina, which had been the organ of his government. It was the voice of Mitrist liberalism and one of the great dailies of the country; it published novels as serials, such as Julián Martel's La Bolsa, and had correspondents including writers such as José Martí and Rubén Darío.

fuentes/la-nacion/por_que_importa.texto: For more than a century it was one of the most influential dailies in Argentine politics and culture.

fuentes/el-obrero/resumen.texto: Socialist newspaper that appeared in December 1890 as the organ of the country's first workers' federation, edited by Germán Avé-Lallemant until 1892. It analyzed the 1890 crisis and the Argentine economy with Marxist categories, presented the country as a capitalist economy subordinated to foreign capital, and defended the political organization of workers.

fuentes/el-obrero/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the first Marxist newspapers in Latin America.

fuentes/la-vanguardia/resumen.texto: Socialist newspaper founded by Juan B. Justo and a group of militants on April 7, 1894, which in 1896 became the organ of the Socialist Party. It defended the political and trade-union action of workers, reform through parliament, free trade and the naturalization of immigrants so that they could vote.

fuentes/la-vanguardia/por_que_importa.texto: It was the main voice of Argentine socialism for decades.

fuentes/la-protesta/resumen.texto: Anarchist newspaper founded in Buenos Aires in 1897 as La Protesta Humana, which in 1903 took the name La Protesta and later became a daily. It defended anarchist communism, direct action and the general strike, supported the FORA, and was shut down and attacked several times, among them during the Centennial of 1910, when nationalist groups set fire to its print shop.

fuentes/la-protesta/por_que_importa.texto: For three decades it was the main organ of anarchism in Argentina and one of the most widely read in the Hispanic world.

personas/mitre/resumen.texto: Porteño military officer, politician and historian. Governor of Buenos Aires from 1860, he defeated the Confederation at Pavón (1861) and was the first president of the reunified nation (1862–1868); he commanded the allied armies in the War of the Triple Alliance until 1868. He founded the newspaper La Nación in 1870, led the revolution of 1874 and in 1891 agreed with Roca on the electoral pact that divided the Unión Cívica.

personas/luis-saenz-pena/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer and Supreme Court justice, elected president in 1892 as the candidate of the agreement between Roca and Mitre, which sought to block the candidacy of his son Roque. With no party of his own and a hostile Congress, he faced the radical revolutions of 1893 and resigned in January 1895.

personas/jose-evaristo-uriburu/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Salta, vice president of Luis Sáenz Peña, who assumed the presidency in January 1895 after his resignation and completed the term until 1898. His government carried out the second national census (1895), faced the arms race with Chile and in 1898 promulgated the constitutional reform.

personas/manuel-quintana/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer and politician, interior minister of Luis Sáenz Peña during the repression of the revolutions of 1893 and Argentine delegate to the Pan-American conference in Washington (1889–1890). President from 1904, he faced the radical revolution of February 1905 with the state of siege and died in office in March 1906.

personas/figueroa-alcorta/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Córdoba, vice president under Quintana, who assumed the presidency upon his death in 1906 and completed the term until 1910. He dismantled Roca's electoral network with federal interventions and in January 1908 had the police close the extraordinary sessions of Congress; his government celebrated the Centennial. He later presided over the Supreme Court (1929–1931), so he was the only person to head all three branches of the state.

personas/victorino-de-la-plaza/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Salta, finance minister and foreign minister in governments of the conservative order and vice president under Roque Sáenz Peña. He took office in 1914, upon Sáenz Peña's death, kept the country neutral in World War I and in 1916 handed power to Hipólito Yrigoyen, the first president elected under the secret and compulsory voting law.

personas/dalmacio-velez-sarsfield/resume.texto: Jurist from Córdoba, author with the Uruguayan Eduardo Acevedo of the Commercial Code of Buenos Aires (1859), which the nation adopted in 1862, and author of the Civil Code, which Congress approved in 1869. He was finance minister under Mitre and interior minister under Sarmiento.

personas/adolfo-alsina/resumen.texto: Porteño politician, son of Valentín Alsina and leader of the Partido Autonomista, who in 1862 opposed the federalization of the province of Buenos Aires. He was governor of Buenos Aires (1866–1868), vice president under Sarmiento and war minister under Avellaneda, where he pushed the southern frontier forward and ordered the ditch that bears his name dug; he died in office in 1877.

personas/carlos-tejedor/resumen.texto: Porteño jurist, author of the draft Penal Code that served as the basis for the 1886 code. As governor of Buenos Aires (1878–1880) and a presidential candidate against Roca, he armed provincial militias and was defeated in the June revolution of 1880; he resigned, and the city of Buenos Aires was federalized.

personas/bernardo-de-irigoyen/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer and diplomat who had served Rosas's government. As Avellaneda's foreign minister he signed the 1876 boundary treaty with Paraguay, and as Roca's foreign minister the 1881 treaty with Chile; he later was a leader of the Unión Cívica Radical and governor of Buenos Aires (1898–1902).

personas/rufino-de-elizalde/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer and politician, foreign minister under Mitre from 1862 until his resignation in September 1867, and later under Avellaneda. He signed the Triple Alliance treaty for Argentina on May 1, 1865 in Buenos Aires.

personas/mariano-varela/resumen.texto: Journalist born in Montevideo, son of Florencio Varela, director of the Buenos Aires daily La Tribuna and foreign minister under Sarmiento (1868–1870). In an 1869 note to the government of Brazil he held that victory did not give the allies the right to fix the boundaries with Paraguay on their own, a position contrary to the letter of the 1865 treaty.

personas/marcos-paz/resumen.texto: Politician from Tucumán, vice president under Mitre, who governed while Mitre commanded the armies in Paraguay. He died of cholera in January 1868, during the epidemic that reached Buenos Aires from the front.

personas/aristobulo-del-valle/resumen.texto: Lawyer and national senator, one of the founders of the Unión Cívica and civil leader of the 1890 revolution together with Alem. In 1893 he was the most influential minister of Luis Sáenz Peña: his decision to disarm the militias of some provinces facilitated the Radical uprisings of July, which according to several historians he had prepared with Yrigoyen, and he had to leave the government a few weeks later.

personas/dardo-rocha/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer and politician, governor of Buenos Aires (1881–1884), who founded La Plata in 1882 as the new capital of the province after the federalization of the city of Buenos Aires. He later became the first rector of the provincial university of La Plata (1897).

personas/indalecio-gomez/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Salta and Catholic politician, interior minister of Roque Sáenz Peña. He prepared with him the enrollment, electoral roll and secret and compulsory voting laws, and defended them in Congress in 1911.

personas/pablo-riccheri/resumen.texto: Military officer from Santa Fe, war minister under Roca between 1900 and 1904. His 1901 law imposed compulsory military service on men aged 20 and reorganized the army during the arms race with Chile.

personas/luis-maria-drago/resumen.texto: Porteño jurist, foreign minister under Roca in 1902–1903. Faced with the blockade of Venezuela by Great Britain, Germany and Italy, he held in a December 1902 note that the public debt of a state does not authorize armed intervention or the occupation of its territory: the Drago Doctrine. He later served as an arbitrator at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague.

personas/carlos-calvo/resumen.texto: Diplomat and international law scholar who spent almost his whole career in Europe in the service of the Argentine government. In his Theoretical and Practical International Law (1868) he held that foreigners cannot claim more protection than nationals nor ask their governments for armed intervention to collect their claims: the Calvo Doctrine.

personas/francisco-solano-lopez/resumen.texto: Son of Carlos Antonio López and president of Paraguay from 1862. Facing Brazil's intervention in Uruguay, he ordered the capture of the Brazilian steamer Marquis of Olinda (November 1864), invaded Mato Grosso and in April 1865 the Argentine province of Corrientes, and carried on the war until he died at Cerro Corá in 1870. Liberal historiography presented him as a tyrant who provoked the war; Paraguayan nationalism and Argentine revisionism, as a defender of his country's sovereignty.

personas/venancio-flores/resumen.texto: Caudillo of the Uruguayan Partido Colorado, who had fought alongside Mitre at Pavón. In 1863 he invaded Uruguay from Argentine territory against the Blanco government, received military support from the Empire of Brazil in 1864, and entered Montevideo in February 1865; as provisional ruler he signed the Triple Alliance, and he was assassinated in Montevideo in 1868.

personas/duque-de-caxias/nombre.texto: Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, Duke of Caxias

personas/duque-de-caxias/resumen.texto: Brazilian soldier, commander of the imperial forces in the Paraguayan War from late 1866 and allied commander after Mitre’s departure in 1868. He directed the siege of Humaitá, the December 1868 campaign that ended at Lomas Valentinas, and the occupation of Asunción in January 1869.

personas/jose-eduvigis-diaz/resumen.texto: Paraguayan general who commanded the defense of the Curupaytí trenches, where the Allied assault was repulsed on September 22, 1866. He died in 1867 from wounds received during a reconnaissance on the Paraguay River.

personas/chacho-penaloza/resumen.texto: Federalist caudillo of the Llanos de La Rioja, a former officer of Facundo Quiroga. He rose up twice against the liberal governments that followed Pavón: the 1862 uprising ended with the Treaty of La Banderita, and the 1863 one with his defeat and his death at Olta, where he was killed after having surrendered.

personas/pablo-irrazabal/resumen.texto: Military officer born in Uruguay, serving the national army, and commander of one of the columns that pursued the montonera of Chacho Peñaloza. On November 12, 1863, at Olta, he killed Peñaloza, who had surrendered shortly before, and his head was displayed in the town square.

personas/felipe-varela/activo.lugar.texto: San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

personas/felipe-varela/resumen.texto: Estanciero and military officer from Catamarca, an officer under Chacho Peñaloza. At the end of 1866 he returned from Chile with a proclamation against Mitre and the Paraguayan War and led the federal rebellion of the west; defeated by Antonino Taboada at Pozo de Vargas (1867), he continued the struggle in the north until 1869 and died in exile in Chile in 1870.

personas/antonino-taboada/resumen.texto: Military officer from Santiago del Estero who, with his brother Manuel, dominated the politics of Santiago del Estero from 1851 as an ally of the liberals and of Mitre. On April 10, 1867, he defeated Felipe Varela at Pozo de Vargas, on the outskirts of La Rioja.

personas/jose-miguel-arredondo/resumen.texto: Uruguayan-born officer in the Argentine army, who fought the montoneras, defeated Juan Saá at San Ignacio (1867), and fought in Paraguay. In the 1874 revolution he rose up in the interior in support of Mitre and was defeated by Julio A. Roca at Santa Rosa (Mendoza).

personas/ricardo-lopez-jordan/resumen.texto: Entre Ríos caudillo, lieutenant of Urquiza and opponent of his rapprochement with Mitre and Sarmiento. After Urquiza’s assassination in 1870, which was attributed to him, the legislature elected him governor, and he led three rebellions against the national government (1870-1871, 1873, and 1876); he was murdered in Buenos Aires in 1889.

personas/miguel-cane/resumen.texto: Writer and politician of the Generation of '80, author of Juvenilia (1884) and En viaje (1884). He was a diplomat, mayor of Buenos Aires, and senator, and in 1899 he presented the bill that became the Ley de Residencia in 1902, also known as the Ley Cané.

personas/eduardo-wilde/resumen.texto: Hygienist physician and writer born in Tupiza (Bolivia), a figure of the secular liberalism of the Generation of '80. As Roca’s minister of Justice, Worship, and Public Instruction (1882-1886), he defended Ley 1420 in Congress, and as minister of the Interior under Juárez Celman, the civil marriage law of 1888.

personas/lucio-vicente-lopez/resumen.texto: Lawyer and writer born in Montevideo, son of the historian Vicente Fidel López, author of the novel The Big Village (La gran aldea, 1884). He was a deputy and minister of government during the federal intervention in Buenos Aires in 1893, and he died in a duel in 1894.

personas/eugenio-cambaceres/resumen.texto: Lawyer, deputy, and novelist from Buenos Aires. He introduced Zola’s naturalism into the Argentine novel with Pot-pourri (1882), Sentimental Music (1884), Aimless (1885), and In the Blood (1887).

personas/julian-martel/resumen.texto: Journalist from Buenos Aires for the newspaper La Nación who, under the pen name Julián Martel, published the novel The Stock Exchange (La Bolsa, 1891), about the speculation that led to the crisis of 1890.

personas/paul-groussac/resumen.texto: Writer and historian born in Toulouse, who arrived in the Río de la Plata in 1866. He directed the Biblioteca Nacional from 1885 until his death, founded the journals La Biblioteca and Anales de la Biblioteca, and was the most influential critic of his time; he wrote From the Plata to Niagara (1897) and historical studies of Liniers and of Mendoza and Garay.

personas/jose-manuel-estrada/resumen.texto: Catholic writer, professor, and orator from Buenos Aires, rector of the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires. In 1884 he led the Catholic opposition to Ley 1420 and to Roca’s religious policy and founded the Unión Católica; because of his criticism of the government he was removed that year from the rectorship and from his chairs.

personas/pedro-goyena/resumen.texto: Lawyer, journalist, and Catholic deputy from Buenos Aires. In the debate over the 1883 education law he defended religious instruction in public schools against Wilde and Onésimo Leguizamón, and with Estrada he founded the newspaper La Unión and the Unión Católica.

personas/onesimo-leguizamon/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Entre Ríos, minister of Justice and Public Instruction under Avellaneda, and judge of the Supreme Court. He presided over the 1882 Pedagogical Congress, and as a deputy in 1883 he defended the secular common education that Ley 1420 enshrined.

personas/joaquin-v-gonzalez/resumen.texto: Jurist and writer from La Rioja, governor of La Rioja (1889-1891) and Roca’s minister of the Interior, for whom he prepared the draft national labor law in 1904. As Quintana’s minister he founded the Universidad Nacional de La Plata (1905), which he presided over until 1918; he wrote The National Tradition (1888) and My Mountains (1893).

personas/jose-maria-ramos-mejia/resumen.texto: Physician from Buenos Aires, organizer of the Asistencia Pública de Buenos Aires (1883) and president of the Departamento Nacional de Higiene and, from 1908, of the Consejo Nacional de Educación, where he promoted patriotic education. From positivism he read Argentine history through psychiatry and the psychology of crowds in The Neurosis of Famous Men, Madness in History (1895), The Argentine Crowds (1899), and Rosas and His Time (1907).

personas/carlos-octavio-bunge/resumen.texto: Jurist, sociologist, and writer from Buenos Aires with a positivist training, professor at the University of Buenos Aires. In Nuestra América (1903) he explained the problems of Spanish America by racial mixture and inherited character, with the racial determinism common in the social science of his time.

personas/juan-agustin-garcia/resumen.texto: Jurist, judge, and professor from Buenos Aires. In The City of the Indies (La ciudad indiana, 1900) he studied colonial Buenos Aires society through law, economics, and customs, one of the founding works of social history in the country.

personas/ricardo-rojas/resumen.texto: Writer born in Tucumán and raised in Santiago del Estero. In The Nationalist Restoration (1909), a report to the government on education, he proposed a historical and patriotic education to integrate the children of immigrants; in 1913 he founded the chair of Argentine literature at the University of Buenos Aires, of which he was rector from 1926 to 1930.

personas/manuel-galvez/resumen.texto: Writer born in Paraná, secondary education inspector, and novelist. In The Diary of Gabriel Quiroga (1910) he defended a Catholic and Hispanic nation against cosmopolitanism and immigration; he later wrote The Normal School Teacher (1914) and was one of the inspirations of nationalism and historical revisionism.

personas/estanislao-del-campo/resumen.texto: Poet and civil servant from Buenos Aires, a supporter of Mitre, who signed as Anastasio el Pollo. His Fausto (1866), in which one gaucho tells another about a performance of Gounod’s opera at the Teatro Colón, is one of the major works of gauchesco poetry.

personas/hilario-ascasubi/resumen.texto: Gauchesco poet born in Fraile Muerto (Córdoba), a soldier of the Unitarians and an enemy of Rosas, who from Montevideo produced propaganda in verse with his characters Paulino Lucero and Aniceto el Gallo. In 1872 he published in Paris his great poem Santos Vega, or The Twins of La Flor.

personas/eduardo-gutierrez/resumen.texto: Journalist from Buenos Aires who published, in serialized installments in the newspaper La Patria Argentina, novels about gauchos pursued by the law, the most famous being Juan Moreira (1879-1880). Its adaptation as a circus pantomime with José Podestá (1884) lies at the origin of Río de la Plata theater.

personas/florentino-ameghino/resumen.texto: Self-taught naturalist born in 1853 in Moneglia (Italy), according to a letter of his own, who was brought as a child to Luján and who, with his brother Carlos, assembled large collections of fossils from the pampas and Patagonia. In The Antiquity of Man in the Plata (1880-1881) and Phylogeny (1884) he defended evolution and the very ancient presence of human beings in the region; his thesis that humanity had originated in South America was rejected by later science. He directed the Museo Nacional de Buenos Aires from 1902.

personas/eduardo-holmberg/resumen.texto: Physician and naturalist from Buenos Aires who studied Argentine flora and fauna and directed the Jardín Zoológico de Buenos Aires between 1888 and 1904. He was also a pioneer of science fiction and detective fiction in the country with The Marvelous Journey of Mr. Nic-Nac (1875), Two Parties in Conflict (1875), and The Bag of Bones (1896).

personas/hermann-burmeister/resumen.texto: German naturalist, director of the Museo Público de Buenos Aires from 1862 until his death. At Sarmiento’s request he organized the Academia de Ciencias de Córdoba, with professors brought from Germany, and he was an opponent of Darwin’s ideas.

personas/benjamin-gould/resumen.texto: American astronomer hired by Sarmiento’s government, first director of the Observatorio Nacional de Córdoba (1871-1885). With his assistants he cataloged the stars of the southern sky in the Argentine Uranometry (1879), and in 1872 he organized the Oficina Meteorológica Argentina.

personas/pedro-scalabrini/resumen.texto: Italian educator and naturalist settled in Entre Ríos, professor of history, philosophy, and sciences in Paraná from 1872. He assembled large fossil collections, and the history of ideas identifies him as the disseminator of Comte’s positivist philosophy among the teachers of the Escuela Normal de Paraná.

personas/amadeo-jacques/resumen.texto: French philosophy professor who went into exile after Louis Napoleon Bonaparte’s coup (1851) and arrived in the Río de la Plata in 1852. As director of studies of the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires (1863-1865) he prepared the curriculum that the national colleges followed; Miguel Cané recalls him in Juvenilia.

personas/juana-manso/resumen.texto: Writer and educator from Buenos Aires, exiled during Rosas’s government, who collaborated with Sarmiento on common education. She directed schools and the journal Anales de la Educación Común, founded popular libraries, and defended secular schooling and the education of women.

personas/guillermo-rawson/resumen.texto: Physician and politician from San Juan, Minister of the Interior under Mitre (1862-1868). He was the first professor of public hygiene at the University of Buenos Aires and in his Estudio sobre las casas de inquilinato de Buenos Aires (1885) he described the conditions of the conventillos; he died in Paris in 1890. The city of Rawson, founded by the Welsh colonists of the Mimosa on 15 September 1865, is named after him because he was the minister who had agreed with them to settle in Chubut.

personas/francisco-javier-muniz/resumen.texto: Military physician and naturalist, considered the first Argentine paleontologist for his fossil finds in Luján; Darwin cited his observations on ñato cattle. He died in 1871, infected with yellow fever while caring for the sick; the Buenos Aires hospital for infectious diseases bears his name.

personas/jose-roque-perez/resumen.texto: Lawyer born in Córdoba, founder of the Argentine Grand Lodge of Freemasons (1857). He presided over the Popular Commission that organized care for the population of Buenos Aires during the 1871 yellow fever epidemic, and he died after contracting it.

personas/cecilia-grierson/resumen.texto: Teacher from Buenos Aires who in 1889 graduated from the University of Buenos Aires as the first woman physician in the country. She founded a nursing school, promoted child care, kinesiology, and the civil rights of women, and presided over the First International Women’s Congress (1910).

personas/julieta-lanteri/resumen.texto: Physician born in Italy and raised in La Plata, and a feminist activist. In 1911 she obtained Argentine citizenship through the courts, registered on the municipal electoral roll, and on November 26, 1911 she voted in the municipal elections of the city of Buenos Aires; she is considered the first woman to have voted in Argentina.

personas/juan-bialet-masse/resumen.texto: Catalan physician, lawyer, and builder who settled in the country in 1873 and who, with Carlos Cassaffousth, built the San Roque dam in Córdoba. In 1904, at the request of Minister Joaquín V. González, he toured the interior and wrote the Report on the State of the Argentine Working Classes.

personas/german-ave-lallemant/resumen.texto: German surveyor and geologist who drew the first topographic map of San Luis. A Marxist, he founded in 1890 the newspaper El Obrero, which analyzed the Argentine economy with the categories of Capital, and he was a candidate on the first list of the Partido Socialista.

hechos/presidencia-de-mitre/resumen.texto: Mitre took office on October 12, 1862 as the first president of the reunified nation, seated in the city of Buenos Aires under the compromise law that left federalization pending. He organized the federal courts and the Supreme Court, created the national colleges, adopted the Commercial Code and commissioned the Civil Code, while the national army repressed the montoneras of the interior; from 1865 he led the war against Paraguay. For liberal historiography it was the organization of the national state; for the federalists of the time and for revisionism, the imposition of Buenos Aires by force of arms.

hechos/presidencia-de-sarmiento/resumen.texto: Sarmiento took office on October 12, 1868. He ended the Paraguayan War (1870), carried out the first national census (1869), promulgated the Civil Code, founded the Escuela Normal de Paraná, the Córdoba Observatory, and the Academy of Sciences, created the Comisión Protectora de Bibliotecas Populares (1870) and, with the Ley de Subvenciones of 1871, allocated national funds to the schools of the provinces. He faced the yellow fever epidemic of 1871 and the López Jordán rebellions in Entre Ríos, and at the end of his term the Mitrist revolution of 1874 broke out.

hechos/presidencia-de-avellaneda/resumen.texto: Avellaneda took office on October 12, 1874, in the middle of the Mitrist revolution, which his government defeated. He faced the economic crisis of 1874-1876 with a harsh adjustment to pay the foreign debt, sought reconciliation with Mitre, enacted the Ley de Inmigración y Colonización (1876), and directed the frontier campaigns of Alsina and of Roca, which reached the Río Negro in 1879: the state occupied the lands of the Indigenous peoples of the pampas and of northern Patagonia, and thousands of Indigenous people died or were taken prisoner. His term ended with the revolution of 1880 and the federalization of the city of Buenos Aires.

hechos/presidencia-de-roca/resumen.texto: Roca took office on October 12, 1880, with the motto “paz y administración” (peace and administration), at the head of the Partido Autonomista Nacional. His government unified the currency (1881), signed the boundary treaty with Chile of 1881, extended the railways and state control over Patagonia and the Chaco with new military campaigns against the Indigenous peoples, and enacted the Ley 1420 of common education and the civil registry law, which led to the break with the Vatican in 1884. His critics denounced the government’s control over elections and succession.

hechos/presidencia-de-juarez-celman/resu.texto: Juárez Celman took office on October 12, 1886 and concentrated leadership of the Partido Autonomista Nacional, a hegemony that his opponents called the “unicato.” His government enacted the Ley de Bancos Garantidos (1887) and the Ley de Matrimonio Civil (1888), sold state-owned railways, and presided over a great boom in credit, immigration, and speculation. The crisis of 1890 and the revolution of the Parque forced him to resign on August 6, 1890.

hechos/presidencia-de-pellegrini/resumen.texto: Pellegrini, Juárez Celman’s vice president, took office on August 6, 1890 in the middle of the financial crisis. He assembled a loan from Buenos Aires banks and merchants to pay the debt maturities, created the Caja de Conversión (1890) and the Banco de la Nación Argentina (1891), and negotiated a moratorium with external creditors. In 1891 he supported the agreement between Roca and Mitre that split the Unión Cívica.

hechos/presidencia-de-luis-saenz-pena/re.texto: Luis Sáenz Peña took office on October 12, 1892 as the candidate of the agreement between Roca and Mitre. With no party of his own, he changed cabinets several times, and in 1893 he faced the Radical revolutions in Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, and San Luis, which he suppressed with federal interventions and a state of siege. He resigned on January 22, 1895 for lack of support in Congress.

hechos/presidencia-de-jose-evaristo-urib.texto: Uriburu took office on January 23, 1895 after Luis Sáenz Peña’s resignation. His government carried out the second national census (1895), bought weapons amid tensions over the boundaries with Chile, and in 1898 enacted the constitutional reform that updated the basis of representation of the deputies and raised the number of ministries to eight.

hechos/segunda-presidencia-de-roca/resum.texto: Roca returned to the presidency on October 12, 1898. He fixed the value of the peso with the Ley de Conversión (1899), established compulsory military service (1901), restored relations with the Vatican (1900), and closed the boundary conflict with Chile with the Pactos de Mayo and the British arbitration award of 1902. In the face of workers’ strikes he enacted the Ley de Residencia (1902) and, at the same time, commissioned the Bialet Massé report and the draft national labor law (1904).

hechos/presidencia-de-manuel-quintana/re.texto: Quintana took office on October 12, 1904 and in February 1905 defeated the Radical revolution with a state of siege. His government enacted the Ley de Descanso Dominical (1905) and nationalized the University of La Plata at the initiative of his minister Joaquín V. González. He died in office on March 12, 1906.

hechos/presidencia-de-figueroa-alcorta/r.texto: Figueroa Alcorta took office on March 12, 1906 upon Quintana’s death. He clashed with Roca’s faction in Congress, intervened in provinces, and in January 1908 had the police close the extraordinary sessions and extended the budget by decree. His government created the Departamento Nacional del Trabajo (1907), reserved for the state the oil found at Comodoro Rivadavia, and celebrated the Centenary of 1910 under a state of siege.

hechos/presidencia-de-roque-saenz-pena/r.texto: Roque Sáenz Peña took office on October 12, 1910, elected without competition by the network of governors of the conservative order, and set out to end electoral fraud. With his minister Indalecio Gómez he enacted general enrollment and the military roll (1911) and the Ley 8871 of secret and compulsory voting (1912), with which the Radicals returned to the elections and won in Santa Fe and in the Capital. Ill, he delegated command to Victorino de la Plaza in October 1913 and died on August 9, 1914.

hechos/presidencia-de-victorino-de-la-pl.texto: Presidency of Victorino de la Plaza

De la Plaza, acting vice president since 1913, took over the presidency upon the death of Roque Sáenz Peña in August 1914. He maintained Argentina’s neutrality in the First World War, faced the collapse of foreign trade, and carried out the third national census (1914). He guaranteed the elections of 1916, the first presidential elections under the Ley Sáenz Peña, which were won by Hipólito Yrigoyen.

hechos/presidencia-de-francisco-solano-l.texto: Francisco Solano López succeeded his father in October 1862 and governed with absolute powers, relying on a large army and on a state that owned vast tracts of land and held the monopoly on the export of yerba mate. From late 1864 he took the country to war against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay, which ended with his death at Cerro Corá on March 1, 1870.

hechos/intervencion-brasilena-en-el-urug.texto: The Brazilian envoy José Antônio Saraiva delivered an ultimatum on August 4, 1864 to the Blanco government of Atanasio Aguirre, and on August 30 Paraguay warned that it would consider the occupation of Uruguay an attack on the balance of power in the Plata. In October Brazilian troops entered Uruguay in support of Venancio Flores, took Paysandú after a siege (January 2, 1865), and Flores assumed the government in Montevideo in February 1865.

hechos/campana-del-mato-grosso/titulo.texto: Capture of the Marqués de Olinda and Invasion of Mato Grosso

hechos/campana-del-mato-grosso/resumen.texto: On November 12, 1864 a Paraguayan vessel captured the Brazilian steamer Marqués de Olinda on the Paraguay River, which was carrying the new president of the province of Mato Grosso. At the end of December Paraguayan forces invaded that province, took the Coimbra fort, and in January 1865 occupied Corumbá. It was the beginning of the war between Paraguay and Brazil.

hechos/invasion-paraguaya-de-corrientes/.texto: Mitre denied Paraguay passage through Argentine territory to attack Brazil, and the Paraguayan Congress authorized war against Argentina in March 1865. On April 13, 1865 the Paraguayan fleet captured two Argentine steamers in the port of Corrientes, and its troops occupied the city; the formal notice of war reached Buenos Aires only after the attack. On May 1 Argentina, Brazil, and the government of Flores signed the Triple Alliance.

hechos/guerra-de-la-triple-alianza/titul.texto: War of the Triple Alliance (Paraguayan War)

hechos/guerra-de-la-triple-alianza/resum.texto: The war began when Paraguay responded to the Brazilian intervention in Uruguay by capturing the Marqués de Olinda (November 1864) and invading Mato Grosso and, in April 1865, Corrientes; Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay signed the Triple Alliance. After the Paraguayans were expelled from Corrientes and Rio Grande do Sul (1865), years of trench warfare followed at Tuyutí, Curupaytí, and Humaitá. The Allies occupied Asunción in January 1869, and the war ended with the death of López at Cerro Corá on March 1, 1870, with Paraguay devastated and an enormous loss of population. Liberal historiography blamed López; Argentine, Paraguayan, and Brazilian revisionism (León Pomer, among others) held Mitre, Brazil, and British interests responsible; and historians who later worked with the diplomatic archives, such as Francisco Doratioto and Thomas Whigham, reject the British role and explain the war by the conflicts among the states of the region over Uruguay, the rivers, and the borders.

hechos/publicacion-del-tratado-secreto/t.texto: Publication of the Secret Treaty of the Triple Alliance

hechos/publicacion-del-tratado-secreto/r.texto: The 1865 treaty was secret, but the Uruguayan foreign minister Carlos de Castro gave a copy to the British minister in Montevideo, William Lettsom, who in June 1865 sent it to London. The British government printed it and presented it to Parliament in 1866. When the clauses on the territories that Paraguay was to cede and the commitment not to negotiate with López became known, Bolivia, which claimed part of the Chaco, and other American governments protested, and opposition to the war grew in Argentina.

hechos/batalla-del-riachuelo/resumen.texto: On June 11, 1865 the Brazilian squadron under Admiral Barroso defeated the Paraguayan fleet on the Paraná River, off the Riachuelo stream, near Corrientes. Paraguay lost control of the rivers, which isolated its troops in Argentine and Brazilian territory.

hechos/desbandes-de-basualdo-y-toledo/re.texto: On July 3, 1865 most of the militiamen whom Urquiza had gathered at the Basualdo stream camp, in the north of Entre Ríos, to march against Paraguay dispersed and returned to their homes; in November, gathered again, they disbanded at Toledo. They were the most visible sign of opposition to the war in Entre Ríos, which historians attribute to hostility toward Brazil after Paysandú and to distrust of the government in Buenos Aires.

hechos/batalla-de-yatay/resumen.texto: On August 17, 1865 the Allied vanguard under Venancio Flores annihilated, near the Yatay stream close to Paso de los Libres, the Paraguayan column of Pedro Duarte, which had advanced along the Argentine bank of the Uruguay River. Duarte was taken prisoner, and the Paraguayan column on the other side of the river was left isolated in Uruguayana.

hechos/sitio-de-uruguayana/resumen.texto: The Paraguayan column of Antonio de la Cruz Estigarribia, which had invaded Rio Grande do Sul, was besieged in Uruguayana after Yatay. It surrendered on September 18, 1865 to Emperor Pedro II, Mitre, and Flores, ending the Paraguayan offensive in Allied territory.

hechos/batalla-de-tuyuti/resumen.texto: On May 24, 1866 the Paraguayan army attacked the Allied camp at Tuyutí, in southern Paraguay, and was repulsed with enormous losses. It is considered the largest pitched battle fought in South America; thousands of soldiers died, most of them Paraguayan.

hechos/conferencia-de-yataity-cora/resum.texto: On September 12, 1866 Mitre and Francisco Solano López met at Yataity Corá, between the lines of the two armies. López proposed negotiating peace, and Mitre replied that the Triple Alliance treaty prevented any agreement that did not include his departure from government; the war went on.

hechos/batalla-de-curupayti/resumen.texto: On September 22, 1866 the Allied army under Mitre assaulted the Paraguayan trenches of Curupaytí, defended by José Eduvigis Díaz, and was repulsed. The official Allied count gave about 4,000 casualties, dead and wounded, split almost evenly between Argentines and Brazilians (some contemporary accounts gave double that or more), against a few dozen Paraguayan dead. Among the dead was Domingo Fidel Sarmiento, Sarmiento’s adopted son. The defeat halted the Allied offensive for ten months, until July 1867, and increased opposition to the war in Argentina.

hechos/sitio-de-humaita/resumen.texto: The Humaitá fortress, which closed the Paraguay River, withstood the Allied siege between 1866 and 1868. In February 1868 a Brazilian squadron forced its way past it on the river; in July the garrison evacuated it, the remnants of its defenders surrendered in early August, and the Allies demolished its fortifications as the 1865 treaty required.

hechos/campana-de-diciembre-y-lomas-vale.texto: December 1868 Campaign and Battle of Lomas Valentinas

In December 1868 the Allied army under Caxias encircled the Paraguayan positions south of Asunción and defeated them at Itororó (December 6), Avay (December 11), and Lomas Valentinas (December 21 to 27). The Paraguayan army was nearly destroyed, but López escaped into the interior and continued the war.

hechos/ocupacion-de-asuncion/resumen.texto: In the first days of January 1869 Allied troops, mostly Brazilian, entered Asunción, which had been evacuated, and the city was looted. In August 1869 the Allies installed a provisional Paraguayan government, while López resisted in the northern sierras.

hechos/batalla-de-acosta-nu/resumen.texto: On August 16, 1869, at Acosta Ñu, a Paraguayan force made up largely of children and adolescents, with few adult soldiers, was destroyed by the Brazilian army of the Count of Eu while it covered López’s retreat. In Paraguay, August 16 is remembered as Día del Niño (Children’s Day).

hechos/batalla-de-cerro-cora/titulo.texto: Combat of Cerro Corá and Death of Solano López

hechos/batalla-de-cerro-cora/resumen.texto: On March 1, 1870 a Brazilian force surprised, at Cerro Corá in northeastern Paraguay, the last group accompanying Francisco Solano López, who died in the fighting after refusing to surrender. His death ended the war.

hechos/perdidas-de-poblacion-del-paragua.texto: Population Losses of Paraguay in the War

Paraguay came out of the war with its population greatly reduced, above all adult men, owing to combat, hunger, and epidemics; a count taken in 1870-1871 recorded about 221,000 inhabitants, most of them women and children. Estimates of the losses are highly disputed. Thomas Whigham and Barbara Potthast (1999), starting from an 1846 census and that count, calculate a population of 420,000 to 450,000 before the war and a loss of 60 to 69 percent; Jan Kleinpenning puts it at more than half, while Vera Blinn Reber (1988) argued that the losses had been greatly exaggerated and proposed much lower figures. The highest figures in circulation, of up to 90 percent of the population, rest on an 1857 census that present-day demographers consider invented by the Paraguayan government.

hechos/levantamientos-del-chacho/resumen.texto: After Pavón, the liberal governments installed in the interior with support from the Buenos Aires army pursued the federalists, and Peñaloza rose up in the Llanos of La Rioja in 1862; that uprising ended with the Treaty of La Banderita (May 30, 1862). In 1863 he rose again, invaded Córdoba and San Juan, and was defeated. Mitre’s government entrusted the repression to Sarmiento, governor of San Juan, as director of the war, and, according to the correspondence between the two, Mitre ordered that the montoneros be treated as bandits rather than political enemies; summary executions of prisoners took place during the campaign. For the liberal tradition it was the suppression of rural banditry; for Hernández and for revisionism, a war against the federalists of the interior.

hechos/muerte-del-chacho-penaloza/titulo.texto: Death of the Chacho Peñaloza at Olta

hechos/muerte-del-chacho-penaloza/resume.texto: On November 12, 1863, at Olta (La Rioja), Peñaloza surrendered to Commander Ricardo Vera; shortly afterward Pablo Irrazábal, chief of the column that was pursuing him, arrived and killed him, and his head was displayed on a pike in the town square. Sarmiento, director of the war, approved the punishment and later defended it in El Chacho (1868), while José Hernández denounced it as a murder in Vida del Chacho, published weeks later in Paraná. For revisionism it is the symbol of the repression of the federalists of the interior; for liberal historiography, the end of caudillismo in La Rioja.

hechos/revolucion-de-los-colorados/resum.texto: On November 9, 1866 a mutiny of soldiers from a contingent recruited for the Paraguayan War overthrew the government of Mendoza, and the federalists took control of Mendoza, San Juan, and La Rioja with the slogan of ending the war and of ending the governments imposed from Buenos Aires. Mitre returned from the front with troops; Arredondo defeated Juan Saá at San Ignacio (April 1, 1867), and Taboada defeated Felipe Varela at Pozo de Vargas (April 10). It was the last great federalist uprising of the west.

hechos/batalla-de-pozo-de-vargas/resumen.texto: On April 10, 1867, on the outskirts of the city of La Rioja, the national forces of Antonino Taboada defeated the montonera of Felipe Varela, which had to retreat north. The anonymous folk song “La zamba de Vargas” commemorates the battle.

hechos/asesinato-de-urquiza/resumen.texto: On April 11, 1870 a band of Jordanists under Simón Luengo entered the Palacio San José and killed Urquiza; that same day two of his sons were murdered in Concordia. The Entre Ríos legislature elected Ricardo López Jordán governor, and Sarmiento sent the national army into Entre Ríos.

hechos/rebelion-jordanista/resumen.texto: Ricardo López Jordán resisted the national intervention in Entre Ríos from 1870, until his army was defeated at Ñaembé (Corrientes) in January 1871. He rose again in 1873, when he was defeated at Don Gonzalo, and in 1876, when he was taken prisoner. They were the last rebellions of a provincial caudillo against the national government.

hechos/instalacion-de-la-corte-suprema/t.texto: Installation of the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation

hechos/instalacion-de-la-corte-suprema/r.texto: The Supreme Court, organized by Ley 27 of 1862, was installed on January 15, 1863 in Buenos Aires, presided over by Francisco de las Carreras. That same year Ley 48 regulated the jurisdiction of the federal courts and the extraordinary appeal to the Court, which from then on has overseen whether laws and rulings respect the Constitution.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-nacional-de.texto: Founding of the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires

Mitre created the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires by decree of March 14, 1863, on the basis of the old Colegio de Ciencias Morales, with Eusebio Agüero as rector and Amadeo Jacques as director of studies. It was the model for the national colleges that the government opened in the provincial capitals to train the country’s leadership.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-sociedad-rural/ti.texto: Founding of the Sociedad Rural Argentina

hechos/fundacion-de-la-sociedad-rural/re.texto: A group of large estancia owners, among them Eduardo Olivera, its promoter, and José Toribio Martínez de Hoz, its first president, founded the Sociedad Rural Argentina in Buenos Aires on July 10, 1866, to improve livestock raising and agriculture and to defend the interests of rural producers. It organized livestock exhibitions, promoted the crossbreeding of cattle with British breeds, and for decades was one of the most influential associations in the country.

hechos/epidemia-de-colera-1867/resumen.texto: Cholera, which had appeared in the camps of the Paraguayan War, spread in 1867 and 1868 through Corrientes, Rosario, Buenos Aires, Córdoba, and other provinces. In Buenos Aires Vice President Marcos Paz died (January 2, 1868), which forced Mitre to return from the front to take charge of the government.

hechos/sancion-del-codigo-civil/resumen.texto: Congress approved the Civil Code draft by Dalmacio Vélez Sarsfield sight unseen, without debating its articles, under Ley 340 of September 25, 1869, and the code took effect on January 1, 1871. Alberdi had criticized it in 1868 for departing from the Constitution and for its lack of unity, and Vélez replied in writing.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-escuela-normal-de.texto: Founding of the Escuela Normal de Paraná
